name: HELLP syndrome
aliases: haemolysis elevated liver enzymes low platelets syndrome

reference.source: NICE hypertension in pregnancy guidance / Williams Obstetrics
clinicalPearls: HELLP is an acronym for Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets, and is regarded as a severe variant or complication of pre-eclampsia occurring in the late second or third trimester or postpartum

Presentation is frequently non-specific, with malaise, nausea and vomiting, and right upper quadrant or epigastric pain; hypertension and proteinuria may be mild or even absent, which can delay recognition
The haemolysis is microangiopathic, evidenced by a blood film showing fragmented red cells (schistocytes), a raised lactate dehydrogenase, low haptoglobin, and unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
Classification schemes such as the Tennessee and Mississippi systems grade severity chiefly by the platelet count and the degree of enzyme and haemolysis derangement

Serious complications include disseminated intravascular coagulation, placental abruption, acute kidney injury, subcapsular hepatic haematoma with the risk of hepatic rupture, pulmonary oedema, and eclampsia
Definitive treatment is delivery; supportive care includes control of severe hypertension, magnesium sulphate for seizure prophylaxis, and judicious fluid and blood-product management
Corticosteroids are given for fetal lung maturity when preterm delivery is anticipated, but steroids are not a reliable treatment for the maternal syndrome itself
HELLP may develop or worsen after delivery, so vigilant postpartum monitoring is essential, and refractory or atypical cases should prompt consideration of a thrombotic microangiopathy
reference.pathophysiology: HELLP shares the origins of pre-eclampsia: deficient trophoblastic remodelling of the spiral arteries leads to placental ischaemia and release of anti-angiogenic factors, endothelial activation, and widespread microvascular dysfunction. Endothelial injury and platelet activation cause deposition of fibrin in small vessels; red cells are mechanically fragmented as they pass through these narrowed, fibrin-laden vessels, producing microangiopathic haemolysis, while platelets are consumed, causing thrombocytopenia. In the liver, fibrin deposition in the sinusoids and periportal areas obstructs flow and produces hepatocellular necrosis, raising transaminases and, in severe cases, generating intrahepatic haemorrhage, subcapsular haematoma, and the potential for capsular rupture. These processes explain both the diagnostic triad and the multiorgan complications.
additionalDifferentials: Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia without the full HELLP picture
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Antiphospholipid syndrome or a systemic lupus flare
Acute cholecystitis or other hepatobiliary disease
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with platelet count and a blood film for schistocytes
Liver function tests including transaminases and bilirubin
Markers of haemolysis such as lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin
Coagulation screen including fibrinogen to detect disseminated intravascular coagulation
Renal function, urate, and quantified proteinuria
Blood pressure monitoring and cardiotocography for fetal assessment
Hepatic imaging by ultrasound or cross-sectional scanning if a subcapsular haematoma or rupture is suspected
redFlags: Severe or refractory right upper quadrant pain, or sudden shoulder-tip pain and shock suggesting rupture of a hepatic haematoma
A rapidly falling platelet count or evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation
Features of eclampsia such as headache, visual disturbance, hyperreflexia, or seizures
Fetal compromise or suspected placental abruption
reference.prognosis: With timely delivery and intensive supportive care most women recover fully within days of birth, but HELLP carries appreciable maternal morbidity and mortality, notably from hepatic rupture, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and stroke, along with raised perinatal risk and an increased chance of hypertensive disease in future pregnancies.
pitfalls: Excluding HELLP because blood pressure or proteinuria is only mildly abnormal or absent
Attributing epigastric pain to gastritis or reflux and missing hepatic involvement
Relaxing monitoring or discharging too early, as the syndrome can worsen postpartum
Overlooking a thrombotic microangiopathy when derangements persist or worsen after delivery
Aggressive fluid loading that precipitates pulmonary oedema
references: NICE guideline on hypertension in pregnancy
RCOG guidance on severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia
management: Expedite delivery as the definitive treatment, timed to gestational age and maternal-foetal stability, with prompt delivery for advanced or deteriorating disease
Control severe hypertension with agents such as labetalol, hydralazine or nifedipine to reduce the risk of stroke and placental abruption
Give magnesium sulphate for seizure prophylaxis against eclampsia and continue it through the peripartum period
Administer antenatal corticosteroids for foetal lung maturation when preterm delivery is anticipated
Correct coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia with platelet and blood-product transfusion when there is bleeding, profound thrombocytopenia or disseminated intravascular coagulation
Monitor serial full blood count, liver enzymes and coagulation, and evaluate for subcapsular hepatic haematoma or rupture, managing rupture with urgent surgical and interventional-radiology support
Manage in a high-dependency setting with obstetric, neonatal and intensive-care input, continuing surveillance postpartum until laboratory indices normalise
